question: The recent Commission proposal to simplify the Regulation on Deforestation-free Products1 (EUDR) poses a serious and tangible risk to press freedom and the broader cultural and information sector in Europe. The inclusion of finished printed products creates disproportionate burdens for printed content publishers and retailers while contributing nothing to the protection of forests.

There are reports that the Regulation’s overly complex and burdensome requirements are already pushing retailers to threaten to delist press, and that some publishers have already announced plans to withdraw from the EU.

There is also a danger that millions of books will have to be destroyed because the EUDR would prevent them from being imported into the EU, undermining the entire reasoning behind the Regulation’s aim to save forests. Furthermore, printed products are already highly sustainable and form the backbone of Europe’s democratic, cultural and information ecosystem.

While Commission attempts to simplify its most dangerous regulations are always welcome, it is clear that in this instance, much more must be done to protect a critical sector. Will the Commission therefore revisit its EUDR simplification proposal and exclude printed products such as books, magazines and newspapers from Annex I of the Regulation?

Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 of 31 May 2023 on the making available on the Union market and the export from the Union of certain commodities and products associated with deforestation and forest degradation (OJ L 150, 9.6.2023, p. 206, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1115/oj).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.1.2026) The Commission presented a proposal to amend the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR)1 in order to reduce the load on the EUDR Information System and ease the administrative burden for economic operators, while maintaining the Regulation’s environmental integrity. On 4 December 2025, the co-legislators agreed on the revised EUDR2.

The new date of entry into application will be 30 December 2026 for all companies except for most micro- or small operators, for which it will be 30 June 2027. For micro- or small operators already covered by the EU Timber Regulation3, the entry into application will be 30 December 2026.

The amendments to the EUDR limit the obligation to submit due diligence statements to the first operator placing the relevant products on the market. Downstream operators, such as retreading industry or craft businesses, will no longer need to submit due diligence statements, nor to pass on the reference numbers further in the supply chain.
The amendments to the EUDR also introduced a change to Annex I of the EUDR by removing printed books, newspapers, pictures and other products of the printing industry from EUDR product scope.
1 Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023 on the making

available on the Union market and the export from the Union of certain commodities and products associated with deforestation and forest degradation and repealing Regulation (EU) No 995/2010, OJ L 150, 9.6.2023, p. 206–247.

2 Regulation (EU) 2025/2650 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2025 amending Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 as regards certain obligations of operators and traders, OJ L, 2025/2650, 23.12.2025. 3 Regulation (EU) No 995/2010 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 October 2010 laying down the obligations of operators who place timber and timber products on the market, OJ L 295, 12.11.
